items.body: “There are black silences, like thunderclouds, that burst into flashes of music,” H. G. Wells writes in Select Conversations with an Uncle. The phrase finds an almost literal visual counterpart in Jordan Reyes’s cover for Songs for Sad Poets Vol. III: a dense black expanse pressing against a bleached, nearly featureless sky, its uneven boundary resembling storm clouds seen in negative. It also anticipates a pivotal moment in “Sigils of Decay”, when the music comes to such an abrupt halt that, on first hearing, I had to check whether it was still playing. Out of that prolonged absence a low rumble eventually emerges, giving voice to the disquiet that runs through the latest collaboration between Siavash Amini & Eugene Thacker. The three pieces included are dedicated respectively to Vietnamese poet Hàn Mặc Tử, Brazilian Symbolist João da Cruz e Sousa and Austrian poet Nikolaus Lenau, figures connected by the tradition of the poète maudit. “Leprous Doubt”, for Hàn Mặc Tử, opens with dissonant textures, degraded sounds and sudden changes of register. It is unsettling and unsettled, meandering in unforeseen directions and making its discomfort palpable. The music pauses and resumes, pitching antagonistic forces against one another; moments of sweeping grandeur coexist with passages of intimate travail. It repeatedly attempts to steady itself before faltering again. Circular tones eventually lift to reveal the “glowing abyss” of Thacker’s poem, while intensifying drones recede until a solitary, quivering tone remains. “Sigils of Decay”, for Cruz e Sousa, pushes this instability into silence itself. The long interruption at its centre makes the eventual return of sound unusually physical. As the low frequencies slowly reassert themselves, muted fragments accumulate into a dark, suspended mass. Thacker writes of “muted music / woven by / night spiders”, an image that seems uncannily close to what Amini constructs: strands of sound gradually spun into a crepuscular firmament of drones and disarticulated fragments, only to loosen again. The connection with Cruz e Sousa is equally suggestive. His poetry transforms an inexplicable melancholy into a confrontation with the Infinite; Thacker condenses that metaphysical sadness into the colder “Dread of / Infinite space. / Dread of / Distant skies.” At nineteen minutes, “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” is the album’s most expansive piece. Its opening is nocturnal, with celestial voices suspended above slumbering coils of sound. These gradually precipitate into increasingly abrasive textures, yet the music pulls itself back towards a softer harmonic balance. Timbral shifts become more pronounced as the underlying material turns metallic and resonant. Lenau’s recurring world of night, forests, barren landscapes, grief and death finds an oblique counterpart here: the landscape seems to have been emptied of narrative and retained as atmosphere, shadow and distant light. Voice assumes a much greater presence than on the first Songs for Sad Poets, although words never present themselves as intelligible text. Synthetic voices gather into spectral choirs and dissolve into the surrounding music, allowing Thacker’s poems to remain embedded within the pieces without requiring the listener to follow them line by line. The relationship between poetry and sound consequently operates through images, structures and emotional pressure: Hàn Mặc Tử’s diseased bodies and impossible skies, Cruz e Sousa’s metaphysical melancholy, Lenau’s nocturnal desolation. Each piece finally leaves a coda of silence. By then, Reyes’s cover feels increasingly inseparable from the music: darkness occupies most of the field, while its opposite persists beyond its ragged edge. H.G. Wells’s “black silences” provide an apt description of an album where silence continually threatens to swallow the music, yet also provides the space from which it can begin again. To lift the veil on the production process we have spoken directly to Saivash Amini. On the first Songs for Sad Poets, Eugene Thacker’s poems were never actually spoken; the words were translated into sound without becoming voice. On Vol. III, you take almost the opposite route, programming voice-synthesis software to perform the poems and then processing as many as forty voices until language becomes unintelligible. What interested you in bringing the human voice into the project only to erase its legibility again? Do you still think of these pieces as songs, or has the distinction between voice, text and sound become irrelevant? The idea of voice synthesis came out of a conversation with Eugene about his dislike of the human voice and the vocal music he actually liked like Ligeti’s requiem, where micropolyphony, among other techniques, were used to mask the intelligibility of the text and transform the human choir into something entirely different. I have much of the liberty of a large choir in my DAW with voice synthesis software. It’s not actually a human voice, so I can make a sound very modulated and affected when singing. And I can have as many as I want to have, as long as my CPU can handle it, so micropolyphony can be much more extreme and differently intricate. And yes, I do think of these as songs, they are structured around the poem. Just not conventional songs with known musical structures. But that’s when I’m making them. There’s no point trying to find the points of reference to poems if you’re just listening, they are trying to convey the same thing. Listening closely to the three pieces, decay seems to function as a compositional process rather than simply as an atmosphere. “Leprous Doubt” repeatedly loses substance and regains it; “Sigils of Decay” moves through accumulation and withdrawal; and the nineteen-minute “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” forms large masses of sound that gradually weather away, return and finally disappear. This concern with appearance, erosion and reconstitution also seems connected to Eidolon, Caligo and Severed Like the Red Moon, where sounds are made to float, bleed, collapse, be mutilated and reassembled. Has this become a central way for you to think about musical form? Yes and no, I have been more and more putting focus in making structures and out evolving and directional textures made out of different approaches to generating harmony. It’s not all I think about when making pieces but more likely the result of intentional putting together of smaller directional elements of different duration. So the micro is what determines the macro, and a lot of the times I’m thinking of micro. The poets invoked on Vol. III come from very different linguistic and cultural histories: Hàn Mặc Tử and Vietnam’s “Chaos” school, João da Cruz e Sousa and Brazilian Symbolism, and Nikolaus Lenau and the tradition of Weltschmerz. How did you and Eugene Thacker arrive at these particular figures, and what drew you to bringing such different poetic traditions together within the same musical cycle? That’s all Eugene’s side of the project but the thread that links them all is in the Poet Maudit term which the title comes from. They all fit that category. Much of your recent work has begun from literary or historical material: Ibn Sina on eremos, Xavier Villaurrutia on The Sweat of Earth, early Iranian piano recordings and Malakoot on Caligo, as well as Houshang Golshiri on Severed Like the Red Moon. In each case, the source seems to act less as something to illustrate than as a force that changes the way you treat sound. What does literature give you that a purely musical starting point does not, and has worked so closely with Eugene Thacker altered the way you now read a text as a composer? Using literature for my work goes to my first album. Then I have three collaborations with Matt Finney which were based on his reading his poems and sending them to me. Serus had a strong relationship with the writings of Blanchot I can go on… I find using literature gives me a structure and image which I can turn into sound worlds. I can imagine something to convey that image. I find that very exciting but a lot of background work before the project starts is done on purely musical material. Working with Eugene changed my workflow in general and made my relationship with literature deeper than it was before, and it gave me a lot to think about when it comes to making sound that conveys what one word is telling me. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.excerpt: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. items.body: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together. Chkheidze is a Georgian composer and producer based in the Netherlands. Lippok is Berlin, To Rococo Rot, Raster Noton, installation work, decades of treating electronic sound as material that gets layered, cut, reshaped, and left partially unresolved. They met in Tbilisi in 2019 through a workshop program, worked together on Glacier Music II, then built that into Uncontrollable Thoughts, their first joint album for Morr Music in 2025. Morr Music has spent decades in that specific space between electronica, ambient, post-rock, and minimal composition—múm, The Notwist, B. Fleischmann, music where texture and atmosphere carry as much weight as conventional structure. A natural home for this collaboration. The Sky Was Out of Tune pushes further. Eight pieces, titled only with Roman numerals, and they really don’t function as separate tracks so much as sections of one continuous object. That makes sense, the music grew out of a live performance at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie. Everything feels connected by residue. A texture disappears and something remains behind it. A rhythmic idea dissolves into ambience. A metallic sound becomes the thing guiding the next section without announcing itself as such. “I” opens with what sounds like field recording, natural ambience, small bell-like tones, rattling, paper movement, objects handled close to a microphone. Hard to identify exactly what some of those sounds are. Records that begin this way can immediately position themselves as documentary field recording works where the environment becomes the subject. Here the material behaves differently. It’s preparation. Those sounds establish a physical space before synthetic material gets pushed into it. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface :: That becomes one of the strongest ideas running through the record. Chkheidze and Lippok are extremely good at preparing the listener for something before revealing what it is. Ambience gathers density. Distortion arrives gradually. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface before becoming clearer. Metallic sounds enter and disappear like objects moving through the stereo field. No obvious drops. No resolutions. They build toward changes in texture instead, which is a harder thing to make feel earned. Their process on Uncontrollable Thoughts involved long improvisations, selecting ideas afterward, sending projects between one another. Chkheidze contributing drums, piano, vocals. Lippok adding noise, harmony, sometimes reshaping the entire piece. He’s described his production as primarily layering, constructing, collaging, not sitting at a keyboard writing chord progressions. You can hear that philosophy all over this record. Compared to Uncontrollable Thoughts, The Sky Was Out of Tune is more dissolved. The previous album still had recognizable individual pieces—”Bird Song,” “Rainbow Road,” soft beats, organ drones, clear rhythmic personalities moving between tracks. Boundaries here have almost completely disappeared. Uncontrollable Thoughts felt like two musicians improvising compositions. This feels like those same two musicians improvising an environment. The rhythm is still present but behaves more like weather than percussion. Digital texture and ambience overlapping :: Soft electro rhythms surface throughout, especially when the album settles into its more defined sections. Nothing becomes overly forceful. Even when distortion enters it feels incorporated into the ambience rather than placed over it. There are moments that recall the softer edges of early Mille Plateaux material, digital texture and ambience overlapping until it becomes difficult to decide which one you’re actually listening to. The late 90s and early 2000s electronica sensibility is present throughout, that specific understanding that small rhythmic gestures can carry enormous emotional weight if given room. “VII” is the most interesting section on the record and it lasts 35 seconds. The glitches become more exposed, textures start colliding, and suddenly the album sounds like it might move somewhere completely different—like a corrupted transitional file that accidentally became part of the release. Its short duration is what gives it impact. “VII” functions as a doorway into “VIII” rather than a standalone piece. An introduction to the outro. And that tiny moment reveals something about the whole record, Chkheidze and Lippok are comfortable letting an idea exist only as long as it needs to. A texture doesn’t have to develop into a full track. A rhythmic pattern can appear for seconds and disappear. Something can sound important and still never return. The title describes the music unusually well. A sky being out of tune doesn’t mean the environment has collapsed, it means something familiar has shifted slightly enough that you start paying closer attention. That’s what happens here. Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. The Sky Was Out of Tune is available on Morr Music. items.body: A mesmerizing collision of ambient, jazz, electronics and ritualistic textures, this album unfolds like a deep-space journey that never loses its human pulse. Trumpet drifts through electronic vastness Fade In Brighter Age by Pulsar + Demetrio Cecchitelli   Mahorka has a busy schedule and quite an enormous back catalog, covering various electronic music, from ambient to dub, noise and radically experimental. Confirmed sound artists meet new promising ones in the course of indie, challenging music with no regard for major commercial tendencies. I’ve never heard of Pulsar (Leonardo Pucci) before, but I must say he perfectly teams up with Demitrio Cecchitelli. I’m more familiar with the work of Cecchitelli, notably with the sumptuous Empetus (published years ago by Midira). The addition of trumpet player Jacopo Buda to the soundscapes gives an enriched musical meaning to the album, playing the card of instrumental ambient music with partly experimental-jazzy tones and expansive improvs which evolve on dynamic electronic textures. What we can listen to here is nothing less than a furiously enthralling and original musical trip which starts masterfully with the ethno-ritual and spaced-out “Cosmic Dream”. Such a gorgeous piece with its perpetual circular rhythms covered by inspiring and gently minimal trumpet melodic shifts. It is meticulously crafted without being purely ambient, as it conjugates a vast array of influences, from Buddhist-Zen musical attributes to early minimalism and atmospheric, then bassy, chilled-out vibes. It suggests immensity and nature-like vastness, with its colorful timbres resonating in divine harmony. It is a sprawling track with a magnificent development, always suspenseful, melodically ethereal and dynamic. The second track (“Expanding Light”) also operates a nice syncretism and musical dialogue between acoustic ingredients, wind instruments and electronics, but here we enter a more downtempo, softly moving ambience, less lyrical and tripped-out but equally good and perfectly elaborated. The title track (“Fade in Brighter Age”) almost provides a softly moving dream-pop quality, built on guitars, vibrant chords and slowly enveloping wind sequences, largely embracing a lonesome path and a feeling of consciousness at night. All in all, a varied and semi-jazzy atmospheric ambient album with a flowing cinematic edge. Absolutely recommended and easily one of my personal favorites of this year. For fans of John Hassell, Harold Budd, Peter Knight, Loscil, Bersanin Quartett, Nala Sinephro, and Floating Points. Fade In Brighter Age is available on Mahorka. items.body: Mara gets to Germany and does well. She earns, she buys herself a BMW, and what she boasts about is the legroom: now she can spread her legs as far as she likes. Then the car dies on the Autobahn outside Munich. The crisis has eaten her savings, the job has gone and the visa with it, and she is sat in a car she can’t afford to move. “Mara” is the first single from Gastarbeiter, the third album by GORDAN, out on Glitterbeat on 20 November. Singer Svetlana Spajić found the whole story in two lines. A bećarac, ten syllables to a line, the rhyming couplets people trade at weddings and drinking sessions in the Posavina, the farming country along the river Sava in northern Bosnia, one singer calling and another answering back, usually to make a joke or land an insult. Hers was about a woman stuck on the Autobahn in a new car with no money, sending home for someone to come and get her. Spajić wrote the rest. She keeps that couplet running through the whole lyric. Each verse says its line, then says it again with the words swapped round, Mara sliding from the end of the line into the middle. It’s a story being retold, and it gets worse every time. Halfway through, the verb shifts under the repetition and Mara stops whining that she’s been robbed and starts screaming it. By the last verse she’s home in Bosnia with none of the Deutschmarks left, back to the convertible mark, the currency Bosnia brought in after the war and fixed to the German one at one to one. Mara is a gastarbeiter, a guest worker, and there’s a whole tradition of songs about people like her. West Germany coined the word in the 1960s, after Yugoslavia broke with the rest of the socialist bloc and signed a deal to send its workers north, and it stuck in the Balkans as something said behind a man’s back. Those workers sang about missing home, about the shift, about families split by a border and parents left in the village, and that’s the body of song Gastarbeiter takes its name from. On the album sleeve is Gvozden Leaves for Temporary Residence, Mića Popović‘s painting of an ordinary Yugoslav man. Temporary residence was the state’s phrase for going to work in Germany, and Popović, a dissident, put it in the title to mock it. Gordan came together in Berlin during lockdown. Svetlana Spajić brought thirty years of going out to villages across Serbia, Bosnia and Dalmatia, learning the songs from the singers who still hold them, one place at a time, because the next valley sings the same song differently. That work has taken her into projects with Marina Abramović, Robert Wilson and Antony and the Johnsons. Austrian drummer Andi Stecher and German bassist Guido Möbius come out of noise and minimalism instead, and they also work together as GAMS. The three of them made Down in the Meadow for Morphine Records in 2021 and a self-titled album for Glitterbeat in 2024. items._cn_summary: 这是一张关于外籍劳工议题的概念作品，核心取材自波斯尼亚沿萨瓦河地区的传统十音节对唱体裁bećarac，通过一对押韵对句的反复变奏讲述一位名叫Mara的客工从德国返乡的崩溃叙事。歌手Svetlana Spajić以三十年田野采风积累为基础，将南斯拉夫民间歌谣的叙事结构与实验性处理方式结合，乐队成员则来自噪音与极简主义领域，使传统曲调获得新的语境张力。歌词在重复中逐步改变动词重心，从抱怨被劫掠演变为嘶吼控诉，德国马克到波斯尼亚可兑换马克的货币转换构成隐喻。专辑标题与封面画作均指向六七十年代南斯拉夫劳工赴德的集体记忆，是一张植根于巴尔干民间传统、融合田野录音美学与跨领域即兴手法的作品。

items.body: People leave, and time has the appalling manners to keep moving. A night of company gives way to an empty morning; the room that briefly felt habitable becomes a place for counting what has gone missing. For Obychno Odyn, that familiar collapse belongs to a much larger uncertainty, where even the smallest assurances of affection or stability can disappear before we have learned to trust them. The Turin-based coldwave and post-punk project of Ukraine expat Vadym Protsenko explores that precarious existence on the new single “Уходят люди и часы”, a title that can be translated as “People and Hours Pass.” Its accompanying video, premiering here, takes the song’s profound isolation outdoors, into tall grass, wooded paths, and the dark recesses of old stone ruins. A crunchy snare beat marches through a wash of windlike white noise before the bass establishes its brooding, melodic pattern. There is something almost reassuring about that low-end repetition, a foothold beneath a guitar line intent on making the ground uneven. Fuzzy and discordant, the guitar bends into a jagged melody with the pinched, wayward quality of an out-of-tune saxophone. Protsenko’s voice hangs farther back, its ghostly contours extended by cold reverb, as though the words have traveled across an empty building before reaching us. It makes an appropriately spectral opening to October, with enough rhythmic insistence to keep despair on its feet. The Russian-language lyrics describe a life in which direction and meaning are gradually becoming illegible. People and hours depart together, leaving little beyond the silent business of passing time. A burning planet continues to turn while everyone attends to their own concerns; words are thrown away, and even home offers no guarantee of freedom. Against that wider devastation, the possibility of being needed becomes a modest, painfully temporary refuge. The closing lines, translated into English, bring that feeling into focus: “Sometimes, we are needed by someone Sometimes, at night, we are not alone. But then the morning comes And once again, there is not a soul nearby” That repeated “Sometimes” allows a little tenderness into the song, then measures how briefly it lasts. Morning brings the return of the same absence, sharpened by having been interrupted. The bleakness comes from knowing that closeness is possible while having no confidence that it will remain. The video gives that uncertainty a grainy, unsettled physical presence. Guitar and bass performances alternate between daylight beneath the trees and murky passages enclosed by masonry. Close-ups catch faces through branches and long grass; elsewhere, the image turns upside down, briefly dislodging the performers from solid ground. The greenery crowds the frame, making these open spaces feel surprisingly secluded. There is an appealing awkwardness to the musicians’ black clothes against all that growth, as though they have brought the emotional temperature of an empty club into the middle of the afternoon. Watch the video for “Уходят люди и часы” below: Protsenko founded Obychno Odyn in Bucharest in 2025, responding to global upheaval and the situation in his home country. Writing in Russian and English, he draws on the French coldwave of the 1980s, particularly Trop Tard and Bunker Strasse. The eight-song debut album Излияние (Outpouring) followed in 2026, alongside the project’s first live performances in Bucharest, with DJ sets by Corina Sucarov. The solo project expands into a duo onstage: Protsenko handles vocals and guitar, joined by bassist Marcello Aloisio, who became part of the live lineup this year. “Уходят люди и часы” is available now on streaming platforms. Listen below and purchase the single via Bandcamp. items.body: Reflections on Stellar Regions (1967/1995) Around the end of the year 1995, a „new“ album of John Coltrane, posthumous of course, was announced to be released. Alice Coltrane(AC), generally referred to in the press as Coltrane‘s widow and archive keeper, had found a previously lost tape of a 1967 recording date (and given titles to the tracks), we learned. As a relative newbie to modern, avant-garde jazz, you would generally resort to sources like „Das Jazzbuch“ by acclaimed writer J.-E. Berendt from your local public library (in Lower Bavaria, in my case). As to Coltrane’s music, you would probably have already taken Soultrane and Blue Train as a starting point, passed by Giant Steps und initiated yourself into the Impulse-/classic quartet period with, for instance, Live at the Village Vanguard . You would have learned that A Love Supreme was the peak of his creative work and a great milestone of modern jazz in general. Going on further to Ascension , probably tempted by Mr Behrendt‘s description of it „as an orgasm lasting 40 minutes“, it was, however, not for me. It was simply too much for me to take at that time, especially the lack of any „song structure“, I did not find an orgasm, but a collective, cacophonic mess lasting 40 minutes, to be honest. With that background, learning that the announced release, titled Stellar Regions , was originally recorded in 1967, it caught my curiosity nonetheless. Not only was this my birth year, it would also be interesting to see: how had Coltrane developed from 1965 on? And, sadly, we could expect to listen to some of his last recorded music, just five months before his death, Some raw facts: All the music assembled on Stellar Regions was recorded in the Van Gelder Studio in one day’s work on 15 February 1967, and the released material comprises everything recorded in that session*, with his regular group members of that era: AC on piano, Jimmy Garrison (JG) on bass and Rashied Ali (RA) on drums. But at this date in the absence of saxophonist Pharoah Sanders(PS), thus reducing the late period quintet of Live at the Villard Vanguard Again! to a quartet. After this studio date, Coltrane would return there exactly one week later on 22 February for a duo recording with RA ( Interstellar Space ) and in March for three more tracks to be released in late September 1967 on Expression . All but one of the tracks on Stellar Regions were unreleased before (I knew none of it anyway), as #5 Offering had already been used to complete the Expression album. And by the way, the title track #3 (alternate take #9) was an early version of Venus from the duo session with RA one week later. What is going on here? Having my CD copy of Stellar Regions in hand, what did I get? As an obvious statement already from the back of the cover: Shortness. A return to a noticeable format and compositional structure. 11 tracks (including 3 alternate versions) with a maximum length of just under 9 minutes (#1 Seraphic Light ), well … that sounded fairly familiar to me, even compared to a Genesis or Dire Straits LP (which, in the meantime, had found a place a bit farther behind in the rack). On first listen: Conciseness. Cohesiveness. Control, even constraint. The contrast to Ascension and even more so (although unknown to me), the sprawling marathon improvisations of his live 1966 work (the non-stop concerts of the 1966 tour in Japan!), becomes evident from the start. These pieces are tighter and more concise, the emotional bursts more focused. Lyrical clarity. Spiritual atmosphere. Much to my surprise. While intense and free, these pieces are balanced with moments of meditative calm. I found lyrical beauty on #1 Seraphic Light , #5 Offering and #4 Iris - the latter being a gorgeous ballad, pleasant rediscovery on re-listening and easily the most traditionally and melodically accessible track on the album. Is it „free“ jazz“ actually? Is this free jazz, I wondered? While I have no doubt, that this is a true free jazz album and the right stuff for the readers and makers of the Free Jazz Blog , this album still sits quite on the border for me. Needless to say, by February 1967, Coltrane had abandoned traditional chord progressions and swing rhythms. Why it may justifiably be called free jazz: - The protagonist does of course not abandon the extended techniques he had developed over the years - overblowing, shrieking altissimo notes and multiphonics. - RA displays his non-metric drumming and plays multidirectional rhythms, creating a fluid, rolling wave of percussion rather than playing a traditional steady swing beat. - The musicians as a whole are not bound by traditional chord progressions. They play with harmonic openness, outside the conventional harmony. And what makes it distinct from other works of the period, so it may be not: - Unlike his live performances of this time, Stellar Regions has clear, distinct thematic melodies at the beginning and end of most tracks, providing structural anchors. - JG‘s bass playing also acts as a massive anchor. Because he uses repetitive and modal tools to anchor the root note, the musicians never fully detach from a tonal center. - AC‘s chord playing on piano provides a harp-like, meditative harmonic cushion. It is free-form, but it’s deeply melodic and highly tonal as well. Conclusion: Stellar Regions uses the vocabulary of free jazz (energy, microtonality, open rhythm, non-metrical drumming) but pours it into shorter, concise and deeply spiritual tone poems, finding a balance between freedom and structure. Instead of plainly breaking the rules or „tearing down walls“, it is all about using freedom to achieve an emotional and spiritual state. What stands out I like the more lyrical pieces on this album very much. They really define this album and give it a distinct place in Coltrane’s late period timeline. They a show us a side of Coltrane’s final months that makes already a shift to a more spiritual atmosphere. They touch my heart and make me wistfully curious if more of that kind would have come flowing out of that musician. Offering (# 5) is a majestic ballad, the emotional center of the session and arguably the most structurally complete composition on the album. The track opens with a beautiful, hymn-like melody, played on tenor with incredible tenderness, sounding like a religious lament. AC enters with resonant low-register block chords. Coltrane’s solo moves away from the melody into intense, microtonal and split-tones. However, because AC sustains chords instead of playing dissonant clusters, Coltrane’s own fiery playing never sounds angry or harsh, but soulful, like a spiritual cry. The track concludes with a return to the opening theme. By the time the melody returns, the storm has cleared, leaving a sense of exhausted peace. Seraphic Light (#1). If Offering is a grounded prayer, Seraphic Light, the album’s starter, is pure cosmic ascension. While it has a more active, rolling rhythm play from RA, it remains one of the most texturally dense tracks on the album. This track begins not with a saxophone melody but with a rumbling of drums and cymbals from RA. AC establishes a continuous tremolo on the piano, while JG plays an aggressive, bowing bass drone. RA provides a rapid, metrically free tapestry of cymbals and snaredrum hits throughout. When Coltrane enters on saxophone, he plays short, declarative motifs that rise upward in pitch, bypassing a traditional jazz melody entirely. On this track, AC abandons all traditional piano performance boundaries. She does not simply play chords to back up a soloist, but creates a massive swirl of sound. The track builds to a peak where Coltrane‘s solo moves into the stratosphere, played in the extreme altissimo register of his instrument. Yet even throughout this peak, JG‘s grounding bass and AC‘s rolling waves prevent the track from becoming exhausting. It remains radiant and luminous. Does this album show us a path to the (unrealized) future? Now, as this year marks the 100th anniversary of John Coltrane’s birth and these recordings are almost his last notes to be captured on tape, it is a compelling „what if“-question: Where would he likely have moved to from here? Does this February 1967 recording – especially its lyrical core (see above) - give us a blueprint of what would have come? That is open for debate. Coltrane, sadly, recorded this music just five months before his death. We will never definitely know for sure how his music would have evolved if he had lived on. In his Allmusic review (4 ½* by the way), Scott Yanow argues that Stellar Regions offers no real hints of a future path. However, it may as well be stated that these recordings „represent a suggestion of the evolution his music would have taken had his life not been cut so short“ (David S. Wild, author of the liner notes, June 1995). Stellar Regions implies that Coltrane was heading toward a "chamber free-jazz" where total freedom was guided by internal discipline and structured devotion. Also, Stellar Regions suggests that the 1970s version of John Coltrane would have been less aggressive and far more compositional, spiritual and influenced by eastern aesthetics. It would have been intriguing to see him join his wife Alice in making the shift to World and Spiritual Jazz. Coltrane was already moving toward the cross-cultural, transcendent, meditative music of the 1970s, as evidenced in Alice Coltrane‘s ( Journey in Satchidananda , 1971) and Pharoah Sanders‘ albums recorded after his death. This session from mid-February 1967 still proves that avant-garde music can be profoundly beautiful, universal and divine. *The liner notes from June 1995 by David S. Wild confirm that the track To Be , released on Expression , with Coltrane on flute and PS rejoining him on piccolo flute, was not actually recorded on that same date, although being credited to that date on its original release. Also note: a contemporary review in German by Konrad Heidkamp from 09.12.1995, DIE ZEIT 50/1995, is still available for registered readers of DIE ZEIT . --- Klaus Kitzinger, born in 1967 in Landshut, Lower Bavaria, Germany. Still lives and works there in his daytime job as a lawyer specializing in construction law. A faithful follower of FJB, he got his first hold of free jazz as a teenager in the early to mid 1980‘s, when one enthusiastic pub operator actually brought luminaries like Archie Shepp, Sam Rivers, Joseph Jarman, the Sun Ra Arkestra, Jimmy Lyons/Karen Borca and Andrew Cyrille (spelled „Grille“ in the local newspaper) to his provincial hometown. Besides free jazz, he has an interest in (nearly) everything related to Japanese culture, traditional and modern, thanks to being married to Yuka. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: I’m not very familiar with the work of Dick Raaijmakers, the electronic music pioneer who created numerous groundbreaking works of electroacoustic music and music theatre. Listening to his compatriot Thomas Ankersmit’s homage to the great Dutchman, I’m struck by how many of the sounds generated by Ankersmit’s Serge Modular synthesiser resemble the sounds of war: explosions of fuzz, rapid rotating like helicopter blades, machine gun spitting of dirt, thick burning noise… I’d listened a few times before I read that Raaijmakers would’ve been nine years old at the time of the Battle of Maastricht, when Nazi Germany attacked and captured the city of his birth. I’m not sure how relevant this connection is, if indeed there is a connection. Perhaps Ankersmit would point instead to the ways in which the quirks of analogue electronics lead directly to some interesting aesthetic and psychoacoustic effects. Consider, for example, the rapid beepings heard maybe a third of the way through the piece: they interfere with and stumble over one another in ways that are strangely disorienting to listen to. Imprecision and timing errors are here not effaced or swept under the carpet, but rather taken advantage of to create novel sensory experiences. Towards the end of the piece, a two-pitch seesawing pattern and a buzzing that shifts and grows in bandwidth create an unstable, curiously vague impression, an intensity that presses from all points and none. But it’s hard to get over the sense of chaos and even violence that erupts in the middle of the piece, spewing fire and thunder in all directions. It’s hard to detach oneself from its terrorising effect on base instinct in order to perceive the psychoacoustic phenomena at work. And maybe that’s not the point, as Raaijmakers’ interest in theatre, that art form most invested in the suspension of disbelief, suggests. In any case, “Homage to Dick Raaijmakers” is a spectacular, cacophonous tribute to a trailblazer of electronic music, with Ankersmit’s own careful attention to structure and pacing very much in evidence. It’s certainly piqued my curiosity in Raaijmaker’s work and legacy. items._cn_summary: 这是一张向荷兰电子音乐先驱 Dick Raaijmakers 致敬的专辑，由同乡 Thomas Ankersmit 使用 Serge Modular 模拟合成器创作完成。整张专辑呈现出极具侵略性的噪音美学：爆炸般的毛噪声、类似直升机螺旋桨的旋转音效、机枪般的尖锐喷射声，以及密集燃烧的噪音层，构筑出强烈的混乱与暴力感。中段那些快速交错的蜂鸣声相互干扰，产生奇特的失定向听觉体验，将模拟电子设备的不精确性和时序误差转化为新颖的感官效应。Ankersmit 在结构与节奏把控上展现出深思熟虑的安排，使混乱的声响中依然保有清晰的叙事弧线。作品既是对电子音乐拓荒者的礼赞，也是对模拟电路物理特性所引发的声学与心理声学现象的深入探索。

items.body: The broadly ambitious Generate Music is the Prism Quartet's latest project, featuring saxophonists Timothy McAllister (soprano), Zachary Shemon (alto), Matthew Levy (tenor), and Taimur Sullivan (baritone). Formed in 1984, their mission is �To place the saxophone in unexpected contexts, expand the repertoire through new commissions, and challenge audiences.� On this eleven-track, 86-minute set, they do just that. Tyshawn Sorey | Ursula Rucker | Diane Monroe This collection includes the quartet augmented by David Gilmore (Electric guitar), David Krakauer (Klezmer clarinet), Tyshawn Sorey (Drums and percussion), Reuben Rogers (Bass), Ursula Rucker (Vocals and poetry), Susan Watts (Trumpet and vocals), and Diane Monroe (Violin). Through modern jazz arrangements, improvisations,� and spoken word, they seek to �explore the historical, cultural, and creative ties between Black and Jewish Americans.� Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts � The opening track references �A Griot and a Cantor,� the storyteller in West African culture and the worship leader in the Jewish faith. The sonic architecture arrives with �The Unknown Common Ancestor,� which jumps between a World Saxophone Quartet-inspired sound and klezmer music with clarinet and trumpet.� � Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts The striking and authoritative voice of Ursula Rucker narrates �Requiem for AJ.� After a dramatic overture, it sets up the narrative tension that develops across the record. Rucker tells the story of the 1964 murders of civil rights activists James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner near Philadelphia, Mississippi. On the 60th anniversary of this American tragedy, Rucker explains that they went �to register black voters (sigh)� and then she asks us to: Look up the rest of the story if you care Do you... Care? Or do you just... Do you?� With tense dramatic irony, Rucker nonchalantly states, �Poets have queries,� and the recitation ends with emphatic repetition of �Do you?�� This ten-minute powerhouse also features the band at its best with Tyshawn Sorey�s swirling drumming and David Gilmore (not to be confused with his Pink Floyd namesake) offering one of his several fiery guitar solos. It makes a fitting single, representative of the in-your-face right-left punches of improvised jazz and honest stylized performance poetry. Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts Highlighted throughout with bursts of klezmer, often seamlessly blended with funky jazz, the Jewish tradition is especially highlighted on �Lift Every Voice and Sing.� Originally debuted in 1900, this hymn by brothers John Rosamond Johnson and James Weldon Johnson has been called a �Negro national anthem.� Here it is translated into Yiddish by Joshua Woletzshky and sung by Susan Watts, featuring violin by Diane Monroe. �Shall I continue to lie about my sadness to keep you from yours?� asks Rucker on �Let�s All Gather & Go All Together, Shall We,� offering an optimistic way forward in a world of hate. She narrates the story of a young black man in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who is murdered by a Jewish pharmacist, exposing grief but also a way to get beyond it. Here and throughout, the music comments, prods, replies, and exuberantly jams out. Powerful, virtuosic, and close to the bone, Generate Music keeps its promise and takes another giant step in the evolution of the Prism Quartet. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国裔肯尼亚鼓手Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的二人组合Odd Okoddo，携手83岁的传统dodo歌唱家Ogoya Nengo共同录制。评论指出Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手鼓及偶尔的架子鼓构建多层次的合成复合节奏，悄然铺陈于人声之下，使电子声响逐渐显得有机自然，仿佛一直潜藏在传统声线之中。Nengo的加入为音乐注入深厚的传统根基，她与Ratengo在邻近村庄成长，演唱中彼此呼应、追溯共同血脉。专辑呈现了非洲传统民歌与电子实验声响的深度交融，文化在相互回应中既不践踏根源、又使传统获得前卫表达。文中还将其置于更广泛的folktronica场景中，与Chouk Bwa及Nyege Nyege厂牌的作品相提并论，凸显这一全球化跨文化音乐潮流中非洲声音的独特贡献。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 与意大利实验作曲家 Francesco Paolo Paladino 及诗人 Luca Chino Ferrari 合作的专辑《Songs of Compassion》，收录十一首歌曲。音乐以钢琴为核心，辅以弦乐、木管、合成器音层和金属质感音色，结构非线性、模态化，刻意打破西方和声进行的思维定式，类似 Steve Reich 与 Philip Glass 的简约派路径。歌词兼具诗意与现实关怀，延续1960年代抗议歌曲传统，如《Pale Wanderer》剖析威权主义的合谋机制，《Charlottesville》（与已故 Joe Byrd 合作）直面新纳粹游行，另有对死亡与人类宇宙处境的沉思。Moskowitz 的演唱苍老而权威，将哲学性歌词注入方法派演员般的诠释力，钢琴本身成为另一个叙事声部，乐器织体围绕人声构建脉冲、不协和与微光闪烁，呈现出六十年代激进实验精神在当代的回响。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa在意大利Fazioli钢琴厂的音乐厅完成了一场两小时的独奏即兴录音，由此衍生出这张专辑。原始音频为不设限的自由演奏，后期仅以人声采样、打击乐、循环音效和田野录音进行稀疏点缀，保留了即兴的原始呼吸感。Sosa自陈拒绝被任何风格标签定义——无论是爵士、拉丁、timba还是雷鬼顿，他只在意形式本身。专辑延续Thelonious Monk式的创作信条，强调首次录制的自然性与不可重复性。'Less is more'是他贯穿始终的美学准则，通过琴弦的拨弄与延展，将钢琴共鸣腔体的内在声音挖至深处，制作上体现了从极简即兴到精密混音的完整思路，是一位资深音乐人在自由演奏传统下的持续探索。

items.body: Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. An accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation landscape 07 by fields we found / quiet details   Fields We Found is the alias of British musician, mastering engineer and visual artist Alex Gold, who founded the quiet details label in 2023. Following releases on Home Normal, Seil Records, handstitched*, and Ambientologist, Gold has increasingly focused his work on extended listening. The Landscape series grew out of compositions created for his personal meditation practice; over time, the creative process itself also became a form of meditation. Landscape 07, the seventh installment in the series, runs for more than twenty-five minutes. It is an extended live performance constructed from electronic instruments, tape and successive layers of sound. The piece begins almost without a threshold. A broad sound emerges from the haze, already inhabited by tremors, gentle fluctuations and distant trails. During the opening minutes, the music gains weight; the volume rises calmly and glimmers of light move across its surface. From here, Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. “Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined.” ~Mirco Salvadori The presence of tape can be felt in the sound’s internal movement. The notes have porous edges, slight instabilities and a warmth far removed from artificial stillness. Even when everything appears motionless, something continues to shift. The overall balance gradually changes, brighter colours surface and the mass of sound seems to lift. Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined. Gold handles duration with patience and restraint. Each event is allowed to remain long enough to alter our perception of everything around it. In its central section, the piece takes on a darker, more introspective colour. Threads and reflections continue to move through the texture; through headphones, they reveal small lateral movements, like currents. Light then returns gradually and the music expands without losing its composure. This leads to the point of greatest emotional intensity, reached through patient accumulation. The journey feels natural, almost as though it had formed by itself, while retaining the freedom of a gesture made in the moment. The piece asks for a simple kind of openness: to remain, to listen, to give each nuance time to reveal itself and to accept that the inner landscape may change alongside the sonic one. In these passages, distant echoes of German electronic music from the early 1970s begin to surface. The more abstract expanses of Tangerine Dream’s Zeit, the cosmic materiality of early Klaus Schulze and some of Cluster’s suspended atmospheres come to mind in the way timbre becomes form. Fields We Found keeps everything on an intimate, tactile scale. The connection lies in the trust placed in machines, in their natural drift and in the time a sound needs to reveal its hidden folds. Recording the performance directly to tape preserves the element of risk that gives life to such a gradual process. “A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception.” ~Mirco Salvadori An even closer affinity leads to Éliane Radigue. Landscape 07 shares the French composer’s attentiveness to what can emerge from within a prolonged sound and to the variations that appear when the ear stops searching for a melody. The historical and poetic distance remains clear; the surface here is denser and more explicitly ambient. Yet the kind of listening it requires is close to Radigue’s: focused, patient and ready to recognise an event within apparent stillness. Pauline Oliveros’ Deep Listening also comes to mind, particularly in its understanding of attention as an active part of the work, as does Suzanne Ciani, in the gentle way electronic sound can suggest physical movement. Towards the end, the piece begins to subtract. The pressure recedes, its lines grow sparse and what remains reveals its irregularities more clearly. The farewell becomes fragile. The long fade avoids any emphatic sense of closure. A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception. It is an ending fully consistent with the work as a whole: the ear is left to measure the disappearance, while the silence that follows seems to last a little longer. Landscape 07 succeeds because its calmness contains tension. Meditation here has density, pressure and material memory. The instruments breathe, the tapes impart instability and depth, and the studio work preserves the spontaneity of the performance. With each new listen, the hierarchy of details changes: something that first seemed marginal becomes a guide, a fluctuation turns into rhythm, a blur acquires definition. This is music that entrusts its richness to time and draws its strength from time in return. A remarkable entry in the series, and perhaps its most accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation. Landscape 07 is available on quiet details. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是英国音乐人Alex Gold（Fields We Found）创作的《Landscape》系列第七作，时长逾二十五分钟，以电子乐器、磁带与层层叠加的声部构建出一段近乎无门槛的持续展开。乐评详细描述了作品的呼吸感：缓慢的声波推进、重叠、退却、再以微妙变形的形态回归；磁带介质带来多孔的边缘、轻微的不稳定与温暖感，使声音即便看似静止仍在内部持续位移。中段音色转暗、内省，织体中的线索与反射如侧向水流般移动，光线随后逐渐回归。整首作品没有戏剧性手势，依靠持续时间本身改变听者对周围一切的感知，体现了演奏者对时值处理的耐心与克制。

items.body: Irezumi returns with a deeply immersive ambient journey where granular textures, subtle electronic details, and melancholic atmospheres unfold into a beautifully restrained world of sound. Deeply introspective sound waves flowing all around the room   Irezumi is a French-based abstract-minimal ambient music project formed by sound artist Manuel Mesdag back in 2008. His first album, titled Endurance, is highly regarded by passionate listeners in search of beautifully/carefully designed soundscapes where electronic scintillations meet cinematic expressiveness and instrumental repetitiveness. The project has a Japanese name, which reflects its very own musical signature, turned toward inner worlds and ritualistic passages to a state of deep quietness. Irezumi has been highly productive throughout the years, constantly delivering expressive layered soundtracks imbued with a particular flowing meditative mood. This new album makes no exception and reveals a refined body of calm, enchanting, soothing, and sometimes sorrowful granular synthesized textures, augmented by sparse micro-noises and a palette of sonic effects. A track such as “Deliverance” delivers a progressively enveloping and grainy sonic ambient splendor, passing from very quiet to fully opened sounds. The general mood is very evocative, suggesting something at once tense and darkly opaque, yet infused with lighter emotional vibes. Every piece is built on delicate, fragile, spacious, and deeply introspective sound waves flowing all around the room. Among my favorite moments offered by the album, I can mention the ghostly, blurred-out section of the profoundly melancholic “Unstable” or the trippy, mind-travelling and minimal “Shelter”. Perfect accompaniment for moments of self-reliance and easily recommended for fans of ambient electronica with an impressionistic feeling and tasty, minimal-melodiously inclined acoustic sounds. Never disappoints and is of solid musical value. The album is delivered in beautiful vinyl format and distributed by Paris-based indie label Brique Rouge, known for embracing and promoting a vast range of electronic music, with a particular interest in clubbing, house, and techno music. Downfall is available on Brique Rouge. [Bandcamp] Irezumi – Downfall by IREZUMIThe post Irezumi :: Downfall (Brique Rouge) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: What began as an ordinary box of records arriving at work quickly turns into a strange trip down the rabbit hole of Synaptic Cliffs—a label where extraterrestrials, electronic music legends, immaculate vinyl and one very elusive artist called pdqb somehow all make perfect sense.   The box that changed everything “Robert, there’s a box there for you.”“Thanks. I’ll grab it on the way back.” I generally have records delivered to work. Living in Spain, a lesson worth learning quickly is to avoid the post-office unless you have some nostalgia for Soviet Union like queues. “Robert, don’t forget that box.”“No, I’ll be back down.”“Why don’t you take it up with you, out of the way then.”“Right.” Searing Summer heat means that certain jobs, such as carrying boxes up and down flights of stairs, are to be done in one’s own time. But, for some reason, the downstairs gang wanted this box out of sight and out of mind. A nondescript box. Heavy with records, innocent nonetheless. Name. Address of sender. All run of the mill. Perhaps it was the contents; that somehow the sender’s supernatural aura had seeped out from its cardboard cage and given the secretarial staff the heebie-jeebies. Inside, the world of Synaptic Cliffs. Although the return address reads Sascha Dornhöfer, there’s a sense that Pandora herself has put this collection of records together. Nothing chaotic, something mysterious, mystical and bordering on magical. Speaking with Dornhöfer is easy, a pleasure. Pinning down the central artist of Synaptic Cliffs, pdqb, is a story like few others. “pdqb is essentially a character – or maybe something else entirely” So, you are pdqb? Yes, no and maybe. “pdqb is an extraterrestrial who is 127 years old,” and it appears Dornhöfer is “currently possessed by it.” So, you are? “Maybe I’ve only been making music for a few years. Maybe I’ve actually been making music for 30 years. Maybe I’ve already been known under another name. Maybe I’ve been a major producer for other artists. Nobody knows, and nobody is going to find out – at least not through me.” Can you catch heebie-jeebies? This is the story, and Synaptic Cliffs is full of stories. Dornhöfer won’t be held to facts about who he is “because ultimately, this is supposed to be about the music. I don’t want the music to be reduced to a person, a biography, or a recognizable identity. And if people do try to connect everything to a person, then I’d rather give them something so completely absurd that nobody can really make sense of it.” And through the looking glass we go. The label’s style is as difficult to define as its founder. Essentially, the epicentres of this multiverse are pdqb and Perzeptiverdampfkesselqualmtbesinnlich. “pdqb is the main act, mostly electro, but also disco and techno. Perzeptiverdampfkesselqualmtbesinnlich is basically everything else: ambient, experimental stuff, post-punk, scores, soundscapes, that kind of thing.” Ambition is mixed in with the abstract. Opening its doors in 2024, Synaptic Cliffs is now clocking thirty releases across all media with a clear focus on vinyl. Terra firma. Solid ground can also be found when it comes to the connections that pdqb’s music has made with other artists. Legowelt was drafted in for two stellar remixes on the inaugural release Wet Dreams of Jesus Christ with the electro, sci-fi warmth of the original dipped in the delightful haze of Wolfer’s machines. And the names keep coming. Alva Noto, Rolando of Underground Resistance fame, Egyptian Lover, Felix Da Housecat, Umwelt and Roman Flügel with a show-stopping take of “Senftgurken-Prämenöde.” There are also collaborations, the Diskmind EP with Scape One, Guilty Pleasures featuring DMX Krew. And the names keep coming. Reimaginings by Dopplereffekt on Sermons of the Electrofying Messiah. 8½ Bit Replays, a chirpy remix album of the stunning chiptune frolics of 8½ Bit, brings together modern electro masters like PRZ, Galaxian, CEM3340, Dark Vektor and Mesak. New collaborations are on the horizon. Orlando Voorn, Heinrich Dressel and most recently with Edward Ka-Spel, the singer of the Legendary Pink Dots. And… breathe. Where were we? Right, ascending Synaptic Cliffs. “The original compositions are, of course, primarily aimed at the headphone connoisseur listening at home. The remixers are then, so to speak, responsible for the club side of things – although they’re never explicitly commissioned to make something club-friendly. Everyone gets more or less full artistic control. Just like Egyptian Lover, Felix Da Housecat, they can do whatever they want with the track. Of course, you discuss things with each other, but that’s basically how it works.” Just as intriguing as the audio is the visual. The records are beautifully produced, the audio quality singing from the grooves. Art is central. Elaborate swirls and speckled patterns adorn coloured vinyl with sleeves printed to superb quality. And, just like the music, collaborations abound. CONTACT IMMINENT by pdqb & Extrawelt   “Most of them are seriously high-profile artists, people like Maurizio Cattelan (he did the taped banana, an artwork which sold for millions), and Adam Pendleton, and I somehow manage to convince them to get involved” My semi-formed journalistic instincts begin to twitch. Extraterrestrial entities, ok. Million dollar earning modern artists. Hhhmmm?? “By the way, Diskmind (Scape One‘s Quantum Mechanics) was played at Dior’s Spring/Summer Haute Couture show in Paris this year, which made us incredibly happy, because it fit the show perfectly. I’m also a huge fan of Jonathan Anderson.” Wait, maybe my colleagues were on to something. What has this box pulled me into? Fantastical? Supernatural? Whatever this story is, this label, it is definitely one of a kind. Searching for a handrail, let’s get back to the music. “We see ourselves as a premium label. That means no cutting corners anywhere. We work with the best mastering engineers, the records are pressed to the highest possible standards, and the artwork is treated with the same level of care. Everything is done properly.” This is undeniable. But there is also a serious sense of fun to these proceedings. A tongue-in-cheek playfulness that seems to have been lost with the stony-faced seriousness of electronic music or the financial strains of running a label. Dornhöfer is a storyteller, a raconteur who playfully leans into the mysterious with the mischievousness of a boy. The narrative he has woven around Synaptic Cliffs is ever evolving, ever shifting as the imagined somehow takes form.  And that form is very exciting. A label led by a character of boundless energy, an imprint without boundaries, a platform to connect artists and bisect time and space.“I feel another pdqb attack coming……over and out…” Visit https://synapticcliffs.bandcamp.com Cold Calling on the Spirit Line by Perzeptiverdampfkesselqualmtbesinnlich & Edward Ka-SpelThe post Interstellar Seance :: Synaptic Cliffs first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
