items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由瑞典小提琴家与两位挪威乐手组成三重奏，重新诠释斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲。乐评将演奏形容为室内乐式的亲密对话，旋律虽源于民间舞曲，但被刻意解构与碎片化处理，挖掘音乐表面之下的暗流与神秘感。小提琴、高音竖笛与鼓的搭配不追求为舞蹈伴奏，而更接近对传统素材的抽象探索。乐评特别提及开场曲引用挪威Setesdal地区与水妖传说有关的提琴曲，暗示音乐中潜藏的躁动不安。整体呈现出北欧民间素材与实验即兴融合的特征，适合对非传统民谣演绎感兴趣的听众。

items._cn_summary: 为纪念作曲家史蒂夫·赖希九十岁生日，The Quietus发布了其「奇异世界」系列专栏文章，由Sean Kitching撰写，提供十个进入赖希作品谱系的切入点。文章梳理了赖希的代表性创作：从早期磁带相位技术作品《It's Gonna Rain》、简化至双手击掌的《Clapping Music》，到大型合奏作品《Music for 18 Musicians》以及弦乐与磁带结合的《Different Trains》等。这些作品横跨赖希数十年的创作脉络，展现了从极简重复、过程音乐到采样与口述历史融合的多种手法。文章本身是一篇导览性质的长文介绍，并非对单一专辑的深度乐评，但其选题指向当代古典与实验音乐的核心人物，对关注先锋音乐史的读者具有参考价值。

items.body: German electro-industrial project Forma Tadre’s 1996 debut album “Navigator” is available on vinyl for the first time, as the opening release on the new label Analog Frontier. This 30th Anniversary Edition is a 2xLP gatefold pressed on 160g Electric Seaglass Blue vinyl, limited to 300 copies, and is sold through Analog Frontier’s Bandcamp page alongside a digital edition. Analog Frontier describes itself as a label dedicated to pressing CD and digital-only albums to vinyl for the first time, and “Navigator” is its debut release. The gatefold carries entirely new artwork built from period polar-expedition photography. The images include work by Herbert G. Ponting, official photographer of the British Antarctic (“Terra Nova”) expedition led by Robert Falcon Scott. The package also includes a double-sided insert with the album’s full lyrics. Side D of the vinyl edition adds two tracks that have never been released before: “First Land,” recorded in 1995, and “No Gene For Fate,” from 1997. Both date from the “Navigator” era of Forma Tadre’s catalogue. The 13-track edition runs: “Navigator (Part One)” “FX on a Human Subject” “Plasmasleep” “Date Unknown” “Navigator (Part Two)” “Serpent Charmer” “Looking Glass Men” “Mesozoic Tree Ferns” “Gates” “Celebrate the Cult” “Navigator (Part Three)” “First Land” “No Gene For Fate” “Navigator” was written, produced and mixed by Andreas Meyer, the sole member of Forma Tadre. Andreas Torkler handled mastering for the original eleven tracks. Meyer mastered “First Land” and “No Gene For Fate” himself, and Steve Eagle did additional mastering for the vinyl cut. B.A. Donahoo designed the new gatefold artwork, with additional art elements by Jared Cote and Steve Eagle. Hansjoerg Schifferer plays guitar on “Serpent Charmer” and “Celebrate the Cult.” The lacquer was cut at Complete Mastering and the vinyl pressed at Onyx Record Press. Originally released in 1996 on the German label Off Beat, “Navigator” was Meyer’s first release as the sole member of Forma Tadre. The album departed stylistically from the project’s earlier three-piece incarnation. “Navigator” centers on a theme of exploration and combines symphonic instrumental passages with EBM tracks. Meyer’s interest in the occult and in H.P. Lovecraft informed tracks including “Date Unknown,” “Celebrate the Cult,” “Gates” and “Mesozoic Tree Ferns.” The 30th Anniversary Edition is available as a digital album and as the limited vinyl edition on Bandcamp. Shipping of physical copies to the EU is currently on hold due to new EU customs policies. Navigator (30th Anniversary Edition) by Forma Tadre About Forma Tadre Forma Tadre began in 1986 as a three-piece band in Lower Saxony, Germany, with Andreas Meyer among its members. Meyer took the project’s name from a portmanteau of Tangerine Dream’s album “Force Majeure,” after Tangerine Dream’s “Phaedra” prompted him to buy his first synthesizer. The band played live and recorded the EP “Brightful Times” in 1987, produced by German producer Robert “Bobby” Giddens, who had also worked with DAF. Two of the three members subsequently left without recording further material. Meyer was the sole member of Forma Tadre by 1994. After the trio dissolved, Haujobb’s Björn Junemann encouraged Meyer to send demo tapes to record labels, which led Off Beat to sign him. In 1996, Meyer released “Navigator” as his first album under the Forma Tadre name, built partly from songs he had written separately from the band under the working title “P-Songs.” Around 1995, Meyer also worked with a female vocalist on a separate, classically-oriented project named Eisriesenkönig, which released a single track on Off Beat’s 1996 compilation “The O-Files.” After “Navigator,” Daniel Myer of Haujobb approached Meyer to collaborate, and the two formed Newt. The duo released two albums and a single between 1997 and 1999. Through the 1990s and 2000s, Meyer produced remixes for acts including Haujobb, La Floa Maldita, New Mind, Wumpscut and Assemblage 23. Forma Tadre’s second album, “Automate,” followed in 1998 and shifted toward a more ambient sound. After close to a decade of silence, Meyer returned Forma Tadre in 2008 with the 13-track album “The Music of Erich Zann,” inspired by H.P. Lovecraft’s short story of the same name. In 2019, “Brightful Times” was reissued as a hybrid vinyl-and-digital edition that added eight tracks recorded between 1987 and 1992 to the original four-track EP. In 2020, Forma Tadre released two archival anthologies. “Navigator Travelogue” collected remixes, singles, demos and unreleased tracks from 1994-1997, and “P-SongX, the hidden path” gathered personal recordings that predated “Navigator.” In 2021, Forma Tadre released “Geiger’s Day”, its first album issued on CD in 20 years. In 2025, the project followed with the digital archival compilation “Seven Century Factory”, which drew on demos and sketches recorded between 1997 and 2007. This reissue follows the 2019 vinyl-and-digital edition of “Brightful Times.” It extends Forma Tadre’s archival reissue campaign to “Navigator,” the project’s 1996 debut album.

items.body: Review by Second Life Syndrome — Originally written for theprogmind.comThe Emerald Dawn are back with Volume II of their epic, The Land, the Sea, the Air. The band has produced consistently, with increasing quality, over the past decade, and that continues here. This might be my favorite album from them (maybe second favorite after To Touch the Sky). Regardless, more people need to give them a shot.The Emerald Dawn comes to us from St. Ives, UK. They are four-strong, having the same lineup for the last seven years or so. The players are Ally Carter on guitars, soprano and tenor saxophones, and keyboards; Tree Stewart on vocals, keyboards, flute, handSonic, and Roli Seaboard; Dave Greenaway on 6-string bass, and Tom Jackson on drums.They play progressive rock that avoids the cliches. The songs are atmospheric and organic, not to mention quite lengthy. They sound like they could be straight out of the 70s, yet their sound is ever fresh to me simply because they don't really sound like anyone else. Their music is ethereal, mystical, spacious, and even a bit like a folk ritual at times.By now, everything about their sound is like comfort food for my soul: Ally's growling guitars, Tree's illustrious keys and flute, Dave's energetic bass, and Tom intricate drumming. There's a reason why all four of them end up in my top musician features every time they release an album: they are amazingly skilled players who value expression over technicality, authenticity over plasticity. And for my money? Tree has probably laid down the best keyboard performance of the year, swooning and flowing with clarity and majesty. All of the performances are incredible, though.The Land, the Sea, the Air (Vol II) follows the first volume from 2025, which I rather liked. But I think this one is stronger. It has only three songs, in true Emerald Dawn fashion. The first one is called 'Song of the Rainforest', which is twenty-one minutes long. And yet, it is one of my favorite songs by the band to this point. This lengthy instrumental piece is so atmospheric, but somehow also so groovy. The song pulls you into its foliage, and underneath those trees is plenty of searing synth, amazing sax segments, gorgeous melodies, and hypnotic portions that feel otherworldly. I particularly love the precious minutes towards the end that hover with smoky flute, like a spellbinding incense rich with emotion.The second track is 'Rivers of Tears', which is fifteen minutes long. This one took a little more time for me, but I've come to love the focus on piano. It has a bluesy, funk-oriented sound at times, and much of it is reserved and building towards something. The song is structured with more energetic portions in the middle and the end, and each half has its own character, one being piano expressions and the other being more sinister. It's a brilliant track.The final track is called 'Paradise', being about nine minutes long. And you know what? It's yet another favorite from the band. I can't get enough of it right now, actually. It's the most 'normal' song on the album, featuring great vocals from Tree, who also plays her cosmic heart out on the keys. Seriously, this track is both incredibly groovy, almost making me what to dance (almost), but the layers of keyboard melodies, the catchiness of the hook, and the final minutes of sheer instrumental glory are like celestial medicine for the mind. What a finish!The Emerald Dawn are seasoned musicians, yes, but they are passionate artists who truly feel the flow, taste the melody, visualize the color, hear the beating heart of it all. The Land, the Sea, the Air (Vol II) has some of their best work, both calming and foreboding at times. It is a balanced, well-written record that makes you want to start it over again as soon as it ends.
items._cn_summary: The Emerald Dawn 来自英国圣艾夫斯，乐队以四人固定阵容延续了七十年代前卫摇滚的语汇，同时在氛围营造与器乐编排上展现出个人色彩。专辑《The Land, the Sea, the Air》第二卷由三首长篇作品构成：《Song of the Rainforest》以二十分钟器乐曲展开茂密丛林般的声场，合成器、长笛与高音萨克斯交织出仪式感；《Rivers of Tears》以钢琴为轴心，在蓝调与放克律动间缓慢积蓄张力，前后两段分别呈现内敛与阴郁的气质；《Paradise》则将专辑收束于九分钟的冥想式余韵。乐评高度赞赏乐队四位成员的演奏——吉他手粗砺的音色、键盘手的清晰流畅、六弦贝斯的律动感与鼓手的复杂节律共同构成有机整体，避免类型化的俗套，强调表达优先于技术炫耀。整体而言，这是一张回归七十年代前卫精神、注重氛围与旋律而非实验突破的作品，对追求前卫融合或电子跨界听感的听众而言，契合度有限。

items.body: Review by KansasForEver4 — Scotland's most famous band returns in the early fourth quarter of 2026 with its ninth studio album, "A Song for Tomorrow." It is a soundtrack that traverses the Bible, politics, technology, and the (all-too) many conflicts around the globe to explore what lies behind sensationalist media headlines?namely people, their relationships, their emotions, and their experiences."A Song for Tomorrow" presents the dichotomy between our inner selves and the image we project to the world around us: our dreams, the reasons we get up every morning, our falls and recoveries?everything that ultimately defines the human being.PALLAS has chosen a range of themes encompassing environmental collapse, digital surveillance, fracturing relationships, and the unsettling noises of our daily lives. It is a record that showcases the voices of all four band members on equal footing, with each contributing both lead and backing vocals. Did you like the artwork for "The Messenger"? Rest assured, this one is even better; the liner notes reveal nothing about the current hot topic?AI. Mike Bentley is considered the fifth member of PALLAS.The album opens strongly with "Reset" (9/10)?the shortest track on the record, yet one of true beauty that flows effortlessly. It segues into "Rage," a more muscular, almost metallic, and slightly longer track?a piece where Niall Mathewson proves, if proof were needed, that he is a master guitarist (9/10), delivering a sound reminiscent of a wild, Rush-esque soundtrack. "A Song for Tomorrow"?the title track?features the childlike vocals of Natasha O'Neal (who also collaborates with Niall on other musical projects); it is a very calm track until the 4:34 mark, when it intensifies somewhat in the finale, driven by layered backing vocals (9/10). Next up is the epic "The Private Collector," clocking in at over eight minutes; it places Pallas back at the heart of the symphonic progressive rock style the Scottish quartet has mastered since its early days (revisit "The Sentinel" or "The Wedge"?this track is very close to that sound, perhaps leaning more towards the latter). It is a timeless gem?nothing more needs to be said (10/10).The next two tracks, "Dirt" and "Aspirations," are of similar length and tempo; it is hard to say which I prefer. "Dirt" is more accessible and commercial (reminiscent of certain tracks on *The Cross and the Crucible*), whereas "Aspirations" is gentler, featuring quasi-religious backing vocals and Graeme Murray's twelve-string guitar taking center stage (9/10 for the former, 8/10 for the latter). "Rushing Headlong" is far more frenetic?another short piece, and thankfully so, as it was the only track on the album I genuinely disliked; it is chaotic?a term I sometimes use?and messy (6/10).The final three tracks?comprising a third of the album's total runtime?represent the very best of the symphonic progressive rock genre, of which Pallas has long been a leading light. First is "The Avenue of Broken Dreams," featuring a slow rhythmic build-up, Ronnie Brown's atmospheric keyboards, and Niall Matthewson's guitar work?lyrical, inventive, and tastefully restrained. A musical delight (9/10). Then, the shorter, calmer "Mother" (8/10) serves as a breather before what follows: the concluding track, "Inside Outside." This piece distills the very essence of what has defined PALLAS for decades into just over nine minutes. It is a melodic ascent showcasing the musicians at their peak, featuring the kind of soaring lead vocals and magnificent backing harmonies we love, alongside top-tier symphonic elements (10/10).As a side note, the absence of a real drummer didn't bother me in the slightest; Niall and Ronnie split the percussion programming duties depending on the track. It will be interesting to see how this translates to the stage during the band's final tour in a few weeks, as Alan Reed's illness is forcing the Scottish group to cease live performances.

Flesh handles composition and production. “Call Me,” the album’s eighth track, first appeared as a standalone single on 4 September 2026. “Your Blood,” track five, was released as a single in August 2026, ahead of the full album. In its own album notes, the band describes “Dark Bellow” as a dive into “instinct, desire, fear, betrayal, and rebirth,” moving through the “suffocating ghosts of hidden emotions” before closing on what the notes call “the velvet nostalgia of another life.” About Vioflesh Vioflesh formed in Santiago, Chile, at the end of 2017. The project pairs vocalist and lyricist Vio with producer Flesh. The duo works across coldwave and synthpop. darkTunes Music Group signed the band and released its debut album, “Nostalgia,” digitally on 9 May 2025. Young And Cold Records handled the vinyl edition, and Vioflesh issued its own CD and cassette pressings. The 14-track album included “Always,” “Spring Nostalgia,” “So Empty” and “Inside.” Side-Line reviewed “Nostalgia” on release, rating it 8 out of 10. Vioflesh returned with the single “Call Me” on 4 September 2026, followed by “Dark Bellow” on 2 October 2026. The band played US dates this October, including Seattle on 17 October, Portland on 21 October and San Francisco on 22 October. Ticketing listings also show European dates later in the year, including Marseille on 31 October and Rüsselsheim on 17 November, matching the band’s own note that it is “preparing to return to Europe” before the end of 2026.

items.body: ‘Blue Canyon’, by Michael A. Muller (co-founder of Balmorhea), will be releasing a new EP on December 1. Concerned with the specific isolation of wilderness and arriving just in time to take in the snowy elements of the winter season, Blue Canyon offers a respite from the world, thanks to its still and subdued piano. Conceived just before the global pandemic and releasing in the wake of the US presidential election results, the music is a chance to exhale after months of turbulence and unrest. Created during an artist residency at Laity Lodge, in Real County, Texas, which is described as ‘a rugged property down a near-mile drop in elevation in the cedar and caliche wilderness’, Blue Canyon was recorded in purposeful isolation. Although it was recorded in March – a week before the enforced nation-wide lockdown – it could have come from a different era, when the word ‘isolation’ didn’t have the capacity to provoke a panic attack. Muller stayed at the lodge, alone, creating music to fit into and coalesce with the confines of his environment, both spatially and figuratively, intentionally isolating himself within the beauty of the Frio River canyon. He chose to immerse himself in a state of seclusion and isolation, rather than being forced into it by governments, laws, and stay-at-home orders. Nine months later, some people may turn their heads at the thought of having to be alone. But this was not a barricade, or a makeshift prison. It was a chance to be alone – physically, at least, being present among the beauty of nature while retreating from the wider world. Using a Steinway & Sons grand piano and two microphones, Blue Canyon strips everything away – all but the essential. In this way, the music is like a hard reset, providing a sliver of kindness in sketchy times. Choosing facts over illusion and deep, meaningful notes over disinformation and needless clutter, the music is a relief among uncertainty. In fact, the metronomic rhythm, created entirely from the body of the piano, is an assurance, a continuing certainty that relieves pressure and worry and stress. Its incredibly brief nature (the two pieces add up to a total running time of five minutes, making it the shortest record we’ve reviewed) is a sign of the times, with its escapism running into real-world distress as the five-minute-mark comes to an end, but it’s able to feel like a short-but-effective meditation, and exactly what a breather should feel like. On reflection, it’s the perfect length. Any longer and the record would lose its purpose, as well as its strength. There’s a sense of desperate relief in the music – a feeling of breakthrough and the clarifying power of rest. Clarity is a key component of the music. Muller’s largely improvised music was recorded in between solitary hikes through the canyon, and ‘birdwatching at dusk with the soft sway of 100-foot cypress trees rustling in the distance.’ On the final evening of his residency, a thunderstorm broke loose. Sheets of rain and a roaring wind threw echoes at the limestone cliffs. After a storm, though, the air feels cleansed. Blue Canyon feels cleansed, too. It’s the sound of sunshine breaking through and extinguishing a deluge of rain. www.michael-muller.com

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."

His constant exploration of diverse musical languages - in search of new textures and nuances and free from conventional constraints - has led him to expand his sonic palette and reflect it in musical works of very different natures. "The More You Know" (1998), his twelfth studio album, is one of those works that strays furthest from the genre that made Yes one of its leading standard-bearers.Prioritizing gentle, melodic structures over any display of instrumental virtuosity, "The More You Know" moves, almost effortlessly, through pop and world music sounds, in which the arrangements and programming form the foundation upon which much of the album rests. Songs like "Magic Love," "Say Jocky," and "Take, Take, Take" are easy on the ears but don't seem to offer anything substantial. On the other hand, when the English singer's more spiritual side comes to the fore, some of the album's best moments emerge, including the melancholic "Heaven's Love" and "Sad," and the jubilant "Youth" with its ethnic overtones.Also noteworthy are the arrangements on "Dancing Fool" and the light soul-jazz of "Free (Some Would Say)," underpinned by the deep, expressive bass of Bobby Jocky, brother of Francis Jocky, who contributes on keyboards and as a composer. The rest of the album hovers in an accessible average that never quite takes off, with the standout feature being Anderson's angelic voice, which is in fine form. That's no small thing, but it's not enough to overcome a production that, at times, feels overly polished.2/2.5 stars

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Finnish band Von Hertzen Brothers released their fifth studio album 'Nine Lives' in 2013 throughUniversal, having previously caught the attention of the press with the records 'Love Remains theSame' and 'Stars Aligned'. This quintet plays an interesting crossover of pop, prog, and folk,offering an eclectic yet accessible type of rock music that definitely has commercial potential butdoes not shy away from unconventional arrangements. The album 'Nine Lives' in particular issubjected to a high-energy, buzzing start, in the face of melodic numbers like 'Insomniac' and'Flowers and Rust', while its ending resorts to mellower, more atmospheric tones that are exploredon the longer songs 'World Without' and 'Prospect for Escape'. Certain instrumental sections are waytoo loud in the recording, especially in the faster tracks in the beginning, but I think thisproblem is taken care of in the second half of the recording. The vocals are fine, but some of thelyrics feel corny, while the album itself strikes you as almost too eclectic, which is probably whatVHB had wanted to do, but this aspect of it may disengage some listeners. I think the main issuewith 'Nine Lives' is the fact that there are very few highlights present. The record is quite solidoverall and the variety of styles covered provides for an engaging listen, but the songs featured onit are mostly hit or miss.

items.body: Mass Minor, the Austin, Texas-based darkwave and electronic rock project of Andrew J. Martin Jr., released the single “Get Up” on 2 October 2026 via Metropolis Records. Get Up by Mass Minor “This song is a conversation with God at 169 BPM about sin, money, mortality and the things we sacrifice our lives to,” Martin says of the track. “It comes from this idea of asking God to save us from problems we created ourselves. Maybe it’s not God’s job to save us. Maybe we need to fix our own shit. You’re the one holding the light. Get up.” A music video for “Get Up”, directed by Teresa Jolie and edited by Beau Loy, accompanies the release. “Get Up” follows “Nowhere Now”, issued as a single in late July. Both songs are set to appear on a new Mass Minor album, “Beyond The Edge Of Reason”, due out in late February 2027 on Metropolis Records. About Mass Minor Mass Minor is the Austin, Texas-based project of Andrew J. Martin Jr., who blends atmospheric synths and driving guitars with post-punk, synth-pop and alternative rock influences. Martin self-released the project’s debut album, “Become Each Other”, in 2020, followed by a run of singles later collected on EPs. The project built a presence in the dark alternative scene through radio support, multiple SXSW appearances and shows alongside acts including Twin Tribes, Ultra Sunn, TRAITRS, Vision Video, Urban Heat and Sacred Skin. Mass Minor signed to Metropolis Records and released the single “Nowhere Now” in July 2026, followed by “Get Up” on 2 October 2026. Both tracks lead into the project’s next album, “Beyond The Edge Of Reason”, due in late February 2027.

Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album

A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. The duo, Syuri and Sonar, sing in both Japanese and English across the track’s 3:03 running time. An official music video followed on YouTube on October 3, at 20:00 JST (13:00 CEST). The track’s chorus alternates “Han-bun, han-bun, han-bun-bun” (“half, half, half-half”) in Japanese with the English line “Half of me is still asleep.” Each verse plays out as a short back-and-forth: an unfamiliar key in the mailbox, a letter on the fridge that reads only “sorry,” and questions about a name, the time, and whether to go home. The video was uploaded to the duo’s own YouTube channel, @crydopeofficial. “Dark Dopamine” streams on Spotify, Apple Music and other platforms. About Cry DOPE Cry DOPE is the Tokyo-based duo of Syuri and Sonar. The band describes its sound as music that “sits somewhere between a late-night room and the city outside,” sung in both Japanese and English. “Dark Dopamine,” released October 2, 2026, is the duo’s debut single.

items.body: Magic Wands released the single “Guardians” on October 2, 2026 through Metropolis Records. The Los Angeles dream-pop duo of vocalists and guitarists Dexy and Chris Valentine describe the track as a look back at a period that no longer feels real: “This is a song about looking back on a time in your life that doesn’t feel real anymore, even though it really happened.” “Guardians” is the second track lifted from “Sun Kiss,” a new Magic Wands album due in early 2027. It follows “Diamond Rain”, issued in mid-August, which was the first single from the same record. Guardians by Magic Wands “Guardians” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp. Magic Wands’ 2026 singles and EPs “Guardians” and “Diamond Rain” extend a run of releases that started with “Cascades,” the album Magic Wands issued on October 24, 2025. The duo opened 2026 with “Sacred Mirrors,” a January collaboration with Psychedelic Furs guitarist John Ashton. The six-track “Wishing Well” EP followed in April, and Side-Line reviewed it that August. A six-track “Remixes” EP reworking songs from “Cascades” followed in June. Magic Wands remixed Peter Murphy’s “Swoon” in late spring, and Side-Line covered that single when Peter Murphy released “Swoon (Magic Wands Remix)” on May 29, 2026. About Magic Wands Magic Wands formed in Nashville, Tennessee, in the summer of 2008 around vocalists and guitarists Dexy Valentine and Chris Valentine, who began writing together after Dexy moved from Los Angeles to Nashville. The duo later relocated to Los Angeles, where they are now based. Their sound blends dream-pop with shoegaze, post-punk and goth textures, carried by layered guitars, droning synths and Dexy’s vocals. The band debuted with the album “Aloha Moon” (Bright Antenna, 2012), preceded by the EP “Magic Love & Dreams” (2009). “Jupiter” followed on Cleopatra Records in 2016, and “Abrakadabra” on Etxe Records & Productions / Casa del Puente Discos in 2018. Magic Wands self-released “Illuminate” in 2020, then signed to Metropolis Records for “Switch,” released May 12, 2023. Side-Line reviewed “Switch” that September, having already covered the duo’s single “Fortune” in April 2022, the single “Time” that May, and the remix album and tour announced that August. Magic Wands’ sixth album, “Cascades,” arrived in October 2025 and set off the run of singles, remixes and EPs that continued through 2026. “Guardians” now carries that chronology into “Sun Kiss,” the duo’s next album, scheduled for early 2027.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'One Among the Living' is the fourth studio album released by Canadian band Mystery, and to this dayit remains one of their most appreciated and recognizable works. A complex conceptual record, thiselegantly arranged LP offers a melodically-inclined style of neo-progressive rock that is informedboth by the genre's progenitors, and by the glamorous sounds of the 80s AOR/pop rock scene in theUK. Fans of contemporary neo-prog shall recognize many of the traits shared by bands like Pendragon,Galahad, and Arena, in the melodic guitars, opulent keyboard textures, and that fine blend betweensymphonic music and traditional rock instrumentation.The arrangements are intricate and the soundscapes are lush, while the overall atmosphere of 'One Among the Living' seems to be brooding, epic, and even theatrical. And while there certainly are strong ideas with solid execution, 'OneAmong the Living' often feels like something you have already heard, offering familiar sounds thatperfectly fit the neo-prog landscape of the late 2000s. I lack a bit of edge and novelty with thisalbum, even if the emotionally-loaded performances of singer Benoît David are tremendous and praise-worthy. The songs 'Wolf', 'The Falling Man' and the title track might be the strongest entries here,whereas most instrumental sections in 'Till the Truth Comes Out' and 'Through Different Eyes' arequite excellent, too. The rest is way too mellow for my taste, but enjoyers of the neo-prog subgenrewill definitely have plenty of gorgeous material to explore on this 2010 Unicorn Digital release.

items.body:
Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.
Berceuse
Tiny Sun will perform the entire album at Toronto�s Koerner Hall on May 14, 2026.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张时长极短的概念作品合集，共十八首微型小品，总时长仅三十四分钟。制作由三位音乐人远程协作完成，各自拥有独立的音乐背景，其中一位是电视电影配乐作曲家，一位是多伦多民谣乐队主唱，一位以民谣、电子流行及乐队项目知名。乐器配置以拨弦吉他与尤克里里为主，搭配键盘音色与滑棒吉他，整体风格介于美式民谣与室内流行之间。歌词主题围绕失去展开，涵盖失去的爱情与自信，并带有对世界不可测之处的宿命式接受感。专辑在风格上呈现出一定跨度，部分作品具有矿工蓝调气质，另一些则带有灵魂乡村的特质，整体追求极简编曲与歌词的精炼表达。音乐氛围被描述为类似梦境中的声音，朦胧而不确定。
